title: Why a drum is not a string
summary: A drum's overtones are not harmonics: square and circular drums, nodal lines, Bessel zeros, and why where you strike decides what rings.

steps.title: Overtones that don't fit
steps.text:
A string's overtones are harmonics: exactly 2, 3, 4, … times its fundamental, which is why it has a clear pitch. A drum head is a string stretched in two directions, so its modes have two numbers (m, n), and its frequencies are

    f_mn = (c/2) √((m/a)² + (n/b)²),   c = √(T/ρ)

Run this square drum and open Frequencies: the dashed line is where a string's overtones would be. Read f2 / f1 in the Summary.

check.success: √(5/2) = 1.58, not 2. The overtones crowd in at 1.58, 2, 2.24, 2.55, …: no whole-number pattern, so a drum sounds like a thud rather than a note.

steps.title: Nodal lines
steps.text:
Open Mode shapes. Each tile is one mode; the lines through it are nodal lines, which never move. Sprinkle sand on a vibrating plate and it collects on them: these are Chladni patterns. Mode (m, n) has m − 1 nodal lines dividing the width and n − 1 dividing the height.

Start the drum in a single mode: set Start to One mode with m = 2, n = 1, run, and watch the Animation flap either side of the line down the middle.

check.hint: Set Start to One mode, Mode m to 2 and Mode n to 1, then run.
check.success: About 200 Hz, 1.58 × the fundamental. The two halves move in opposite directions and the middle line stays still.

steps.title: A round drum and Bessel zeros
steps.text:
Real drums are round. A circular membrane's modes are Bessel functions J_m(kr) cos(mθ): m nodal diameters and n nodal circles (the rim counts as one). The rim must stay still, so k R must be a zero j_mn of J_m, and

    f_mn = c j_mn / (2π R),   j01 = 2.405, j11 = 3.832, j21 = 5.136, j02 = 5.520

Run the circular drum and compare f2 / f1 with j11 / j01. The Frequencies tab shows the grid's values against the exact ones.

check.success: j11 / j01 = 1.593. The next ones come at 2.14, 2.30, 2.65: again nothing like 2, 3, 4.

steps.title: Strike at the centre
steps.text: Now strike the drum exactly in the middle and open Mode content. The centre lies on a nodal diameter of every mode with m ≥ 1, so a blow there cannot start them.

setup.preset: Circular drum struck at the centre

check.success: Only the axisymmetric modes (0, n) ring, at 1 : 2.30 : 3.60 : 4.90 × the fundamental. They also radiate sound well and die quickly: a centre hit sounds dull.

steps.title: Where you strike decides what rings
steps.text: Move the strike out towards the rim: set Position x to 0.8 and run. Which modes take over?

setup.preset: Circular drum struck at the centre

check.hint: Set Position x to 0.8 (Position y can stay at 0.5) and run.
check.success: The (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), … modes now carry most of the energy. That is why timpanists strike about a quarter of the way in from the rim. In a real kettledrum the air pulls these modes to about 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a missing fundamental, close enough to harmonics to give a clear pitch.
